doc.title: Benny Powell interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Needing the music and not moving to Europe
summary: Woods and Powell on needing jazz, and why Powell never became an expatriate, living in Paris eight months.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Let me ask you this. I want you to come in on this. That is I know I feel this, is that when I listen to Gospel music or I listen to rhythm & blues or I listen to jazz, even though I do enjoy the music tremendously, it seems to go to someplace inside of me deeper than that because the music for me is need based. Actually if I were to spend a year without hearing any jazz, no R&B and no Gospel, I think I’d become ill.

That’s why I didn’t ever move to Europe like an expatriate. I kept on wanting to move to Europe, you know like Benny Bailey and Art Farmer and a lot of those guys did. And I kept procrastinating. Finally I got a chance, I played “Ain’t Misbehavin’.” I lived in Paris for eight months. But I checked myself, and I wondered why I didn’t do it. But it was the same thing. If I woke up hearing [scats] I need to hear some B.B. King. I need to hear some Aretha Franklin. Some Stevie Wonder. Some Dizzy Gillespie and John Coltrane. And if I did that for a year, I don’t think I would have been the same. I believe my playing would have suffered first, but that’s the same point that you have.

The thing is you talk about the aspects of slavery and that was an aspect of denial or deprivation or the stopping you from getting to specific resources that you needed. One you said was if you were thinking in terms of your mother. You were thinking of this person who is a resource for you, who basically in African society took the place of a griot. And so she was your source of knowledge and a source of inspiration and motivation. And so I personally feel that when I’m deprived of something, I use the one thing I do have to try and better my scenario. That’s my musical gift, which makes me play out stronger in a way that’s more authentic than just because I knew the scale out of that textbook. You see what I mean? I wanted to ask you, we’re going to kind of wrap up our interview here, if you have any specific things you’d like to say in closing about jazz education or that you mentioned you’d like to leave something behind to young people. Could you leave us with a statement to inspire or guide young musicians today?
